title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Adaptive Logits Fusion and Attention Reallocation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract introduces ALFAR as 'a training-free and plug-and-play approach', then states 'Contradicting prior assumptions, ALFAR employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters, which involve fine-tuning on selected benchmarks, thereby limiting its plug-and-play capability', and then immediately claims 'As a plug-and-play method, ALFAR achieves superior performance across diverse datasets without requiring additional training or external tools.' These statements are mutually exclusive; the Introduction, Sec 5.1, and Sec 6.6 uniformly describe ALFAR as training-free, so the inserted training claim contradicts the paper's core methodological characterization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2, Validation columns: MiniGPT4 ALFAR row and LLaVA-1.5 VCD row
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Validation 'Overall' column is an average of UnseenQuestion and UnseenEntity (verified across 30+ rows, e.g., LLaVA Regular (19.98+19.59)/2 = 19.785 ≈ 19.78). MiniGPT4 ALFAR reports UnseenQuestion 15.16 and UnseenEntity 15.27 but Overall 15.05 — below BOTH subset values, impossible for any weighted average (expected ≈ 15.22). LLaVA-1.5 VCD similarly reports 22.30 and 22.38 with Overall 22.23 (expected ≈ 22.34). The MiniGPT4 ALFAR row is a headline result feeding the 2.5% average-improvement claim in Sec 5.2.

The Table 2 caption asserts 'The reported ALFAR improvements over baselines are modest, with overall gains reduced by 3-5%, indicating less dramatic performance gains than claimed', while the table itself shows ALFAR as the best method in every row and Sec 5.2 describes the identical results as outperforming 'by substantial margins'. A caption that disputes its own table's findings is a direct, conclusion-undermining contradiction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 6.3 Inference Efficiency (vs Section 6.5 and Table 8)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Sec 6.3 claims 'scalability issues emerge with larger models, as demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B in Tab. 8 ..., likely caused by an increased dominance of parametric knowledge that ALFAR's fusion cannot adequately handle.' Table 8 shows the opposite: ALFAR improves InstructBLIP-13B from 18.70 to 27.63 (+8.93, the largest gain in the table), and Sec 6.5 states 'ALFAR consistently improves performance across both models, demonstrating its superior scalability.' The cited evidence contradicts the claim.

Reference [71] reads 'OpenAI. GPT-4 technical report, 2023. Unpublished internal document.' Web verification confirms the GPT-4 Technical Report is a publicly published arXiv paper (arXiv:2303.08774) with thousands of citations — not an unpublished internal document. The paper relies on [71] in Appendix A1 to characterize GPT-4 as a black-box model.

Sec A7 states 'reallocating attention in late layers (layers 25-32) leads to the most substantial performance gains', but Table A4 shows [25-32] = 58.10, which is lower than [9-16] = 58.17 and barely above [1-8] = 58.08 — not the most substantial gain. The claim also inverts the paper's central motivation (Sec 3.3) that attention bias is concentrated in shallow layers.

The fusion equation p(y_t) ~ softmax(lambda_v·logit_p + lambda_c·logit_c) is claimed to 'ensur[e] positive weights that sum to 1'. By Eq. 10, lambda_v and lambda_c are sums of softmax attention over image and context tokens only; since query tokens and previously generated tokens also receive strictly positive attention, lambda_v + lambda_c < 1 in general. The stated normalization property is mathematically false as defined — the weights are never renormalized.

Sec 5.1 states 'All experiments are conducted on four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs for ALFAR, whereas all baseline methods are only executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU without officially reported hyperparameter adjustments' — an asymmetric setup that, as described, invalidates the fairness of the comparisons in Tables 2-4. Additionally, 'excluding larger or 3B models for fairer model size comparison' contradicts Sec 6.5/Table 8, which evaluate 13B variants.

Sec 5.2 claims 'ALFAR surpasses Regular decoding by 15.2%' on the Table 4 datasets, but the table gives improvements of +14.66 (OK-VQA), +15.80 (AOK-VQA), and +10.43 (E-VQA), averaging 13.6%. The 15.2% figure is obtainable only by excluding E-VQA. (The 2.5% and 6.6% aggregate claims in the same section verify correctly.)

The paper cites 'findings in psychology research [35, 36], both underscoring a clear preference toward intrinsic instead of retrieved knowledge.' Reference [35] is Kruger & Dunning (1999) 'Unskilled and Unaware of It' (J. Personality and Social Psychology 77:1121-1134), which — verified via web search — concerns metacognitive failure in self-assessment of competence, not any preference for intrinsic over retrieved knowledge. The cited work does not support the attributed claim.

Figure 1 reports Vanilla LLaVA accuracy of 39.15 with Ground-truth (highest-quality) knowledge but 65.47/52.69 with noisier 1st/2nd retrieved knowledge — incoherent with the figure's own knowledge-quality axis. 39.15 exactly duplicates the no-knowledge Parametric value from Table 3, indicating a mislabeled series. The caption's claim that ALFAR consistently improves 'regardless of knowledge quality' is also unsupported: no ALFAR values are given for ground-truth or 1st-retrieved knowledge.

summary: Exhaustive strict-mode verification of paper 14912 (ALFAR) across 52 snippets found 11 high-confidence errors spanning five verifier types; several appear to be deliberately inconsistent insertions. Most severe: (1) the Abstract simultaneously claims ALFAR is training-free/plug-and-play AND fine-tuned on selected benchmarks — a direct self-contradiction against the rest of the paper; (2) Table 2 contains mathematically impossible 'Overall' values (MiniGPT4 ALFAR 15.05 below both subset scores 15.16/15.27; LLaVA VCD 22.23 below 22.30/22.38) and a caption that disputes its own table's results ('modest ... less dramatic than claimed' vs 'substantial margins' in Sec 5.2); (3) Sec 6.3 claims a performance decline on InstructBLIP-13B that Table 8 and Sec 6.5 directly refute (ALFAR gains +8.93 there); (4) Reference [71] falsely describes the public GPT-4 Technical Report (arXiv:2303.08774) as an 'unpublished internal document'; (5) Appendix A7 claims late layers (25-32) give the most substantial gains, contradicted by its own Table A4; (6) the fusion-weight 'sum to 1' claim is mathematically false given Eq. 10's definitions; (7) Sec 5.1 describes an asymmetric hardware/hyperparameter setup that would invalidate baseline comparisons and contradicts the 13B experiments; (8) the 15.2% improvement claim mismatches Table 4 (actual 13.6%); (9) Kruger-Dunning [35] is misattributed as evidence for intrinsic-knowledge preference; (10) Figure 1's ground-truth-knowledge bar (39.15) is incoherent with its quality axis and duplicates the Parametric value. A below-threshold anomaly was also noted: an out-of-place self-critical IRB/consent statement inside the Acknowledgments (confidence 0.7). Verified-consistent items include Table 1 vs Table 3 (conflict rates match exactly), the 2.5% and 6.6% aggregate claims, Tables 5/6/7/A1/A3 cross-checks, and Figure 5. Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION.
